## Overview {#overview}

### Research question and objective

Every number on this page comes from synthetic voters: two large language models answering a ballot question while playing Census-shaped Toronto residents. No real person was surveyed.

Toronto elects a mayor and 25 ward councillors on Monday 26 October 2026, and almost no public polling exists for these races. Forecasting from a sample that does not represent the electorate is an old problem [@wang2015forecasting]; here the sample does not contain voters at all. This project therefore asks:

> **Can a *silicon sample* — simulated voters answered by large language models — post-stratified to Census marginals, produce a transparent, reproducible forecast for all 26 Toronto municipal races, and what uncertainty and model disagreement does it imply?**

The forecasting objective is a set of candidate-level vote-share distributions and conditional win frequencies for the mayoral race and all 25 ward councillor races, produced by a fully reproducible pipeline and communicated with honest uncertainty. Following the course framing, we are *not* evaluated on forecast accuracy itself [@gelman2020information on the goals of election forecasts], and nothing on this site should be read as a calibrated prediction of the real election.

The method is *silicon sampling* [@argyle2023out], with the documented perils of LLM survey simulation kept front and centre [@bisbee2024synthetic; @heath2026correcting].

**Pipeline at a glance:**
LLM ballot responses (committed production sample: 3,042 synthetic personas × 26 races × 2 providers × 3 repeats = 36,504 requests, 0 technical failures)
→ census **post-stratification** (decided first-preference shares per race × provider × repeat)
→ **Method C** forecast draws (500 per race × provider: Dirichlet sampling uncertainty + centered multiplicative perturbation, target SD 4pp)
→ provider-specific forecasts, plus a *descriptive* equal-weight pooled summary.

Headline results:

- The **mayoral forecast collapses onto one name**. In the frozen production run both models pick the incumbent, Olivia Chow, in 97.7% of valid mayoral responses, and her main challenger, Brad Bradford, in 0 of 16,406. When the daily tracker shows the same models that day's headlines, the whole electorate swings to whoever the headlines favour (Bradford at 97–99% on 20 October, Chow at 99% on 21 October). The models answer from salience, not from the personas' demographics; see the [Discussion](#discussion).
- Ward races vary substantially, and the **two providers name different leading candidates in 8 of 25 wards** (leader defined by post-stratified point share; see [Provider Comparison](#providers) for the full reconciliation with the alternative definition).
- Forecast uncertainty is **assumption-driven**: widening the assumed perturbation from 2pp to 6pp widens median leader intervals from 33.6pp to 41.0pp — an explicit, documented knob, not an empirical calibration.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Daily Tracker
A fixed 1,200-persona panel is re-polled every morning with that day's Toronto news headlines, and the results are published automatically in the [Daily Tracker](#daily). The frozen forecast on this page does not change.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## What this forecast is — and is not
- **Is:** a post-stratified summary of *what LLMs say* about a Census-shaped synthetic electorate, with model-based uncertainty from repeated sampling.
- **Is not:** a poll, a survey, or a calibrated prediction of the real election. All win numbers are **conditional simulation frequencies**, not probabilities of winning the actual election. See [Limitations](#limitations).
:::

### The mayoral race

![Mayoral vote shares by provider for the eight candidates with the largest pooled shares. Points are census post-stratified estimates of each candidate's share of decided first preferences; bars are 95% simulation intervals. Both providers put almost all support on Olivia Chow.](figures/fig1_mayoral.png){#fig-mayor fig-alt="Dot-and-interval chart of mayoral vote shares by LLM provider. Points are post-stratified point estimates; horizontal bars are 95 percent simulation intervals."}

Post-stratified point estimates (points) and 95% simulation intervals (bars), one row per provider, for the eight mayoral candidates with the largest descriptive pooled shares. Gemini places **Chow, Olivia** at a **99.9%** post-stratified share of decided first preferences; GPT-4o-mini places her at **94.7%** with a much wider personal interval (its repeats vary more and it declines far more often). Under our simulation, Chow's win frequency is **100.0%** (Gemini) and **99.2%** (GPT).

::: {.callout-warning}
## Mayoral mode collapse — read this before quoting any mayoral number
The mayoral forecast is **not** a competitive distribution. In the production silicon sample, Chow absorbs **97.7%** of all valid mayoral choices (99.93% for Gemini, 95.00% for GPT); only 11 of the 53 mayoral candidates are ever chosen. The diagnostic experiment reproduced this under three ballot orders (see [Diagnostics](#diagnostics)), so it is a property of the models rather than of ballot position, the same failure mode documented by @heath2026correcting. No uncertainty method can honestly manufacture competitiveness from it, so the mayoral "forecast" should be read as a *measured model output*, not a horse race. The daily tracker shows that this output is not stable either: the same collapse moves to Brad Bradford when the day's headlines favour him (see [Daily Tracker](#daily) and [Discussion](#discussion)).
:::

One panel per ward. Each panel lists every candidate who is in *either* provider's top two, so both providers' leaders always appear (incumbents marked \*). Rows are ordered by descriptive pooled share, strongest at the top; each provider's point estimate is a dot and its 95% simulation interval a horizontal bar. When a provider's highest dot is on a different row from the other provider's, they disagree about the leader (e.g. Wards 03, 09, 13). Effective sample sizes per ward race and provider are modest (Kish $n_{\text{eff}}$ ≈ 79–165), so ward intervals are wide — typically 30–60 percentage points — reflecting genuine uncertainty *within the LLM response mechanism*. Full per-candidate summaries (all 243 candidates across 26 races) live in `processed/forecast/forecast_summary_centered.parquet`.

## Daily Tracker {#daily}

Every morning a GitHub Action asks the same panel of synthetic Toronto voters how they would vote, after showing them that day's Toronto news headlines. The answers are post-stratified to the Census exactly as in the [Election Forecasts](#forecasts), and this section is rebuilt from the accumulated history.

::: {.callout-important}
## How to read these numbers
These are post-stratified **LLM outputs**, not a poll of real people and not calibrated probabilities. Day-to-day movement reflects how two language models react to that day's headlines. Each persona sees the news fresh each day and has no memory of earlier days. The frozen forecast above does not change when this tracker updates.
:::

### Method {#daily-method}

- **Panel.** A fixed panel of 1,200 personas: 4 drawn (seed 20261020) from each of the 300 ward × age × education census cells of the main forecast's persona frame. Each panel persona carries its cell's population share divided by 4, so ward and citywide weights match the full frame exactly (`R/11_daily_panel.R`). The same personas are asked every day, so changes come from the news context rather than from who is in the sample.
- **Questions.** Each persona answers the mayoral race and their own ward's councillor race, once per model per day: 1,200 × 2 races × 2 models = **4,800 requests a day**.
- **Models.** `google/gemini-2.5-flash-lite` and `openai/gpt-4o-mini` via OpenRouter, temperature 0.7. These are the same models and settings as the frozen production run.
- **News.** Each morning the Action downloads the RSS feeds of CBC Toronto, the Toronto Star (GTA), CityNews Toronto, Global News Toronto, and the Toronto Sun (local news), and keeps up to 12 stories from the last 36 hours. Toronto election stories come first, then other election stories, then everything else, with at most 4 per outlet. Syndicated foreign wire copy is dropped. Headlines and RSS descriptions are used verbatim, with no LLM summary. If fewer than 2 feeds or 5 stories are available, that day is not polled. The day's news file is committed to `processed/daily/news/`.
- **Prompt (v2).** This is the production v1 prompt plus the date, the election date, and the day's headlines (`llm/prompts.py`). As in production, the model only sees the persona's ward, age group, and education group, and the candidate names for one race.
- **Estimates.** Production post-stratification and Method C draws (target SD 4pp, 500 draws per race × model) are run on each day's responses (`R/12_daily_forecast.R`). Headline figures are a 5-day trailing moving average of the cross-model mean, following the Synthetic Voter Project's smoothing choice. Each day has a single repeat per persona and race, so there is more day-to-day noise than in the 3-repeat production run, especially in wards (about 48 panel personas per ward per model).
- **Data.** The full history is in [`processed/daily/history.csv`](https://github.com/Sophiaaa12/toronto-election-forecast/blob/main/processed/daily/history.csv), one row per day × race × model × candidate. Raw responses are in `processed/daily/responses/<date>/`.

### Reconciling two leader definitions

A "leading candidate" can be defined two ways, and they disagree in a few wards because the point estimates and the draws summarise different things (provider point estimates average three repeat cells; win frequencies average 500 draws that resample cells and add uncertainty layers):

| Leader definition | Wards where providers disagree |
|---|---|
| Highest **post-stratified point share** (used on this site) | **8**: W03, W04, W09, W13, W14, W20, W22, W23 |
| Highest **simulation win frequency** | **7**: W03, W04, W14, W15, W20, W22, W23 |

The website uses the **point-share definition** throughout (@fig-wards, @fig-disagree-a, @fig-disagree-b, @tbl-races, and this section). The three definitional edge cases are instructive:

- **Ward 09** — Gemini's point shares are a near three-way tie (Martins, Marco 30.1%; Bravo, Alejandra 29.7%; one other 29.3%), so its top-point candidate is *not* its top-win-frequency candidate. GPT strongly favours the incumbent **Bravo, Alejandra** (82.5%, win frequency 100%), and by win frequency both providers name Bravo.
- **Ward 13** — GPT's point shares are nearly tied (Harris, Morgan 24.7% vs incumbent **Moise, Chris** 24.0%), so GPT's top-point candidate is Harris while its top-win-frequency candidate is Moise; Gemini strongly favours Moise (57.0%). By win frequency both providers name Moise.
- **Ward 15** — both providers' top-point candidate is the incumbent **Chernos Lin, Rachel** (Gemini 48.0%, GPT 73.7%), but across Gemini's three repeat cells the challenger **Sharp, Sheena** leads in the majority of simulation draws (win frequency 58.0% vs 41.8%), so the win-frequency definition flags a split that the point-share definition does not.

Two patterns matter regardless of definition:

1. **Provider disagreement is first-order.** In several split wards one provider gives its leader a win frequency near 90% while the other gives *its* leader only ~35% — disagreement between models is far larger than the difference between any two uncertainty settings ([Forecast Uncertainty](#uncertainty)).
2. **Providers answer differently.** GPT-4o-mini declines ("undecided") far more often, especially in the mayoral race (19.4% vs 0.8% — see [Diagnostics](#diagnostics)), so the providers effectively estimate from different subsets of personas. We therefore report **provider-specific forecasts throughout and never average them into a single "model of models"**; the pooled column elsewhere is explicitly descriptive.

## Forecast Uncertainty {#uncertainty}

Every number on this site comes from an explicit, layered simulation. The four sources of variation are kept distinct, because conflating them would overstate what the data can support. @shirani2018disentangling separate bias from variance in real election polls; our setting has no ground truth against which to make that separation.

1. **LLM response variability** — each draw resamples one of the provider's three independent repeat cells (the same persona-race asked three times at temperature 0.7).
2. **Dirichlet sampling uncertainty** — shares ~ Dirichlet($n_{\text{eff}} \cdot \hat{s} + 0.5$), where $n_{\text{eff}} = (\sum_i w_i)^2 / \sum_i w_i^2$ is the Kish effective sample size of the post-stratified cell. This quantifies how much the estimate would move if the same personas were re-queried.
3. **Assumed forecast perturbation (Method C)** — a centered multiplicative perturbation $s_k \propto s_k \cdot e^{\sigma \varepsilon_k}$, $\varepsilon \sim N(0,1)$, with $\sigma$ calibrated per race so this layer alone gives the leader a standard deviation of the **target SD (4pp default)**. It respects the probability simplex, adds no mass to zero-support candidates, and is only *approximately* center-preserving (realized maximum leader bias across all 52 race × provider units: **5.74pp**, reported rather than assumed away).
4. **Real election uncertainty — not modelled.** No layer accounts for turnout swings, campaign events, polling house effects, or systematic model error shared by both providers.

::: {.callout-note}
## "Win frequency" ≠ "probability of winning"
Throughout this site, **simulation win frequency** means the fraction of 500 model-based draws in which a candidate has the highest simulated share, *conditional on the LLM responses and the assumed perturbation scale*. It is **not** a calibrated probability that the candidate wins the real 2026 election: we have no ground truth to calibrate against, and the source model itself may be systematically wrong. Communicating this gap honestly is the point of the exercise [@gelman2020information; @kay2016when]. Currently 15 of 52 race × provider units show a win frequency of exactly 100%, and 18 of 52 sit at or below 70%.
:::

### Sensitivity to the assumed perturbation scale

![Sensitivity of the forecast to its one assumed parameter, the forecast-noise SD. (a) Each line joins one race-by-provider leader's 95% interval width at SD 2, 4 and 6 percentage points; the dark line is the median. (b) Number of the 52 race-by-provider units whose leader wins every simulation draw; the dark bar is the published setting.](figures/fig5_sensitivity.png){#fig-sens fig-alt="Two panels. Left: leader 95 percent interval widths for all 52 race-by-provider units at target SD 2, 4 and 6 percentage points, shown as thin coloured lines with points and a dark median line rising from 33.6 to 37.3 to 41.0 percentage points. Right: bar chart of the number of units with win frequency exactly 100 percent, falling from 21 to 15 to 12, with the published 4 pp setting highlighted."}

**How to read this figure.** We re-ran the forecast draws three times, changing only one assumption: how much extra forecast uncertainty to add (the target SD, 2, 4 or 6 percentage points). Panel (a) tracks each race × provider leader's 95% interval width across the three settings; every line slopes upward, so the intervals depend directly on this assumed knob. Panel (b) counts how many race × provider units still give their leader a 100% win frequency; that count shrinks as more uncertainty is assumed. Together they show that the *width* of our intervals and how many races look like a certain win are partly a modelling choice, not something the data pins down.

Because the perturbation scale is an assumption, not an estimate, we report a full sensitivity analysis at target SD ∈ {0.02, 0.04, 0.06} (common random numbers, so differences are purely the scale effect). Median leader interval width moves from **33.6pp → 37.3pp → 41.0pp**, and the number of race × provider units with a degenerate 100% win frequency falls from **21 → 15 → 12**. The published forecast uses 0.04; every alternative is committed in `processed/forecast/sensitivity_target_sd.parquet`.

Two further documented uncertainty facts: the Dirichlet +0.5 pseudo-count visibly shrinks leaders toward uniform in small-$n_{\text{eff}}$, many-candidate wards (worst case Ward 19 / Gemini: 5.4% prior mass, ≈ −4.7pp on the leader — affects draws only; point estimates are unaffected), and Method C is only approximately center-preserving (max realized bias 5.74pp, worst: Ward 19 / Gemini).

## Silicon Sampling Diagnostics {#diagnostics}

![Silicon-sample diagnostics. (a) Share of persona-race pairs that pick the same candidate under three different candidate orders. (b) Share of valid mayoral choices going to each of the eight most-chosen candidates. (c) Share of all production responses that were "undecided".](figures/fig6_diagnostics.png){#fig-diag fig-alt="Three panels. (a) Bar chart of candidate-order invariance: 100 percent for the mayoral race for both providers, 56.3 percent for Gemini and 62.5 percent for GPT-4o-mini on 12 sampled ward races. (b) Bar chart of mayoral response concentration: Chow near 100 percent for Gemini, about 95 percent for GPT, with small bars for minor candidates. (c) Bar chart of provider undecided rates: GPT-4o-mini 19.4 percent mayoral and 3.9 percent ward, Gemini 0.8 and 1.0 percent."}

**(a) Candidate-order invariance.** In the diagnostic experiment each persona-race was asked under three ballot orders (the actual ballot order and two randomized orders). The mayoral choice was **100% order-invariant** for both providers — confirming the collapse is knowledge-driven, not a ballot-position artifact. Ward-race choices were invariant in only **56–63%** of complete valid triples (Gemini 56.3%, GPT 62.5%), i.e., ward preferences are meaningfully order-sensitive, a property of LLM survey responses documented by @murray2026choices. We retain it rather than suppress it by randomizing ballot order in production (seed 20261026).

**(b) Mayoral response concentration.** Chow takes 99.9% (Gemini) and 95.0% (GPT) of valid mayoral choices; the remaining mass is spread over ~10 minor candidates.

**(c) Provider undecided rates.** GPT-4o-mini answers "undecided" on **19.4%** of mayoral and 3.9% of ward queries; Gemini on 0.8% and 1.0%. Undecided responses are excluded from estimation by design (the estimand is the decided-voter share), which means the providers effectively condition on different responder pools — the main reason we keep forecasts separate.

Full diagnostic design and verdicts: `docs/llm_diagnostic_experiment.md` and `docs/llm_diagnostic_report.md` (committed).

## Data and Methods {#methods}

### Data sources

All datasets are official City of Toronto sources, downloaded via `download_data.R` with URLs, byte counts, and SHA-256 checksums recorded in `sources.json`:

| Dataset | Use | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Ward Profiles, 25-ward model (2021 Census) [@to2021wardprofiles] | Population frame and post-stratification marginals (ward × age × education) | Toronto Open Data |
| Official 2026 candidate lists (mayor, councillors, withdrawn) [@to2026candidates] | Candidate roster and ballot names for all 26 races | toronto.ca elections |
| Official 2022 election results [@to2022results] | Historical sanity checks; candidate/incumbency context | Toronto Open Data |
| 2023 mayoral and Ward 20, 2024 Ward 15, 2025 Ward 25 by-election results | Updated historical context | Toronto Open Data |
| 2022 Elections Voter Statistics [@to2022turnout] | Ward-level turnout context | Toronto Open Data |
| Wards and Elected Councillors boundaries [@to2026wards] | Map geometry and ward validation | Toronto Open Data |
| Elected officials 2022–2026 | Incumbent identification (name match) | Toronto Open Data |

The Census does not publish an age × education joint distribution, so within each ward we approximate $P(\text{Age}, \text{Education} \mid \text{Ward}) \approx P(\text{Age} \mid \text{Ward})\,P(\text{Education} \mid \text{Ward})$ — an independence approximation documented in the README and carried as a limitation. This yields 12 cells per ward and **300 population cells** citywide (4 age groups × 3 education groups × 25 wards, population 20+).

### Silicon sampling

- **Personas.** 3,042 synthetic personas allocated to the 300 cells proportionally to each cell's share of the citywide 20+ population, with a floor of 5 per cell. Each persona carries its Census design weight (below).
- **Providers and repetition.** Two models through OpenRouter — `google/gemini-2.5-flash-lite` and `openai/gpt-4o-mini` — each queried **three independent times** per persona-race pair at temperature 0.7, max 256 tokens, prompt version v1: 3,042 × 26 × 2 × 3 = **36,504 requests**.
- **Prompt construction.** Each request gives the model only the persona's ward, age group, and education group, plus that race's candidate list (ID + ballot name). It never sees weights, other personas, biographies, policy positions, or historical results. Candidate order is randomized per request (seed 20261026) because LLM choices are order-sensitive (see [Diagnostics](#diagnostics); @murray2026choices).
- **Validation and reliability.** Responses are strictly validated JSON; invalid replies are re-sampled (13 in total); technical failures were retried with backoff and the run finished with **0 technical failures**. Responses are disk-cached (SHA-256 over the full request specification), every request is cost-logged, and a hard budget of $3.75 stopped the run if needed (it was not).
- **Timing.** The pilot and ballot-order experiments ran on the evening of 17 October 2026 (Toronto time). The production run started at 13:35 on 18 October and finished at 23:13 the same night, roughly ten hours of wall-clock time including one interruption and resume; the median request took under one second.
- **Frozen artefact.** The production response file `processed/production/llm_responses.parquet` (36,504 rows) is frozen with md5 `420c3051da6c9a291f5fcf7b587e06bf`; the forecast pipeline halts if it ever changes.

### What the model sees

Each request has a fixed system message (prompt version v1, `llm/prompts.py`) and a short user message. The system message tells the model it is simulating one Toronto resident in a municipal election survey, asks for a JSON reply of the form `{"response_status": "valid_choice" | "undecided" | "not_voting", "candidate_id": ...}`, and instructs it to base its choice only on the candidate names and the respondent's demographics. The user message for persona P000446 and the Ward 4 race reads as follows (shown in ballot order; production shuffles the list per request):

```text
Respond as the following Toronto resident:
- Ward: 4
- Age group: 30-44
- Education group: High school or less

Race: City Councillor for Ward 4 (you are a resident of Ward 4).

Candidates in this race (candidate_id: name):
- W04-C01: Corcoran, Michael
- W04-C02: Guerrera, Nadia
- W04-C03: King, Debbie
- W04-C04: McNally, Diana Chan
- W04-C05: Ogundipe, Bridget
- W04-C06: Pham, Adam
- W04-C07: Potega, Andy
- W04-C08: Raponi, Vanessa
- W04-C09: Weber, Holly
- W04-C10: Yuen, Steve

Return only the JSON object.
```

The daily tracker (prompt v2) adds the date, the election date, and up to 12 of that day's Toronto headlines to the system message.

### Post-stratification

For each race × provider × repeat, over valid (decided) responses only, each persona $i$ carries its design weight $w_i$ (cell population share divided by personas in the cell; weights sum to 1 citywide):

$$\hat{s}_k \;=\; \frac{\sum_i w_i \,\mathbf{1}[\text{choice}_i = k]}{\sum_i w_i}$$

Undecided and not-voting replies are excluded from numerator *and* denominator: the estimand is each candidate's share of **decided first preferences**, not turnout. Ward races sum over that ward's personas; the mayoral race sums over all personas with citywide weights, so wards enter in proportion to their 20+ population.

Provider point estimates average the provider's three repeat cells equally. A separately labelled *descriptive* pooled estimate averages all six cells equally; it is a summary for readers, never used as "the" forecast.

### Software {#software}

The language models are GPT-4o mini [@gpt4omini] and Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite [@geminiflashlite], both reached through OpenRouter [@openrouter]. The query pipeline is written in Python [@python] with requests [@requests] and PyArrow [@pyarrow], and tested with pytest [@pytest]. Cleaning, post-stratification, simulation, and figures use R [@rcore] with dplyr [@dplyr], tidyr [@tidyr], readr [@readr], readxl [@readxl], jsonlite [@jsonlite], digest [@digest], nanoparquet [@nanoparquet], sf [@sf], ggplot2 [@ggplot2], scales [@scales], patchwork [@patchwork], ggrepel [@ggrepel], ragg [@ragg], and systemfonts [@systemfonts]; tests use testthat [@testthat] and code is formatted with styler [@styler]. The site is built with Quarto [@quarto] and set in IBM Plex Sans [@plexsans].

## Discussion {#discussion}

### What a silicon sample measures in a local election

@argyle2023out showed that a language model conditioned on detailed American demographic and partisan backstories could reproduce the vote-choice patterns of the groups those backstories describe, which they called algorithmic fidelity. That result depended on two things this election lacks: party labels that the model can map from demographics to a vote, and a large volume of text linking the two. Toronto's municipal elections have no party labels, and our personas carry only a ward, an age band, and an education band. With so little to condition on, the model falls back on what it knows about the candidates' names. In the frozen run that knowledge is almost entirely about one name: Olivia Chow receives 97.7% of valid mayoral choices and Brad Bradford, whom local coverage describes as her main challenger, receives none of 16,406.

### The collapse follows salience, not demographics

@bisbee2024synthetic found that synthetic survey answers have far less variance than real ones and shift with prompt wording and with the date of the query. Our daily tracker isolates the second effect. Its 1,200 personas, models, and settings are fixed from day to day; only the headlines change. On 20 October, with headlines reporting Bradford pulling ahead, both models gave Bradford 97–99% of decided votes. On 21 October, with headlines about criticism of his water plan, both gave Chow about 99%. A demographic group did not move; the whole synthetic electorate did, at once and in the same direction. This is the mode collapse that @heath2026correcting document, but it is not fixed on the incumbent: it attaches to whichever candidate the context makes salient. It also fits @santurkar2023whose, who found that steering a model toward a demographic group changes its opinion distribution much less than the real gap between groups, and @wang2024misportray, who show that models flatten the variation within identity groups. In our data the persona's age and education barely matter to the mayoral answer.

### Analyst choices are first-order

@murray2026choices show that apparently minor analyst choices change silicon samples substantially. We see the same at every stage we varied. Changing the candidate order changed the ward-race answer for 37–44% of persona-race pairs. Changing the provider changed the leading candidate in 8 of 25 wards. Changing the assumed forecast-noise SD from 2 to 6 points widened the median leader interval by 7 points. Adding a day's headlines replaced the mayoral leader outright. Each of these is larger than the sampling uncertainty that the Dirichlet layer reports, which is why we publish both providers separately and show every sensitivity rather than one blended number.

### What post-stratification can and cannot fix

@wang2015forecasting forecast a US election accurately from a heavily skewed sample of Xbox users, because multilevel regression and post-stratification can reweight a sample that is unrepresentative but still contains real differences between groups. Post-stratification cannot create differences that are not there. When every Census cell gives the same answer, as in the mayoral race, the weights change nothing, and the effective sample is closer to one respondent than to 3,042. Ward races vary more across cells and across providers, so their post-stratified shares carry more information, but that information is about the models. Our conclusion is that, for a low-information local election, a silicon sample is better read as a measurement of what two models find salient than as a survey of voters. Its most useful outputs are diagnostic: where providers disagree, how much the answer depends on ballot order, and how quickly it moves with the news. That is the statement about information sources that @gelman2020information argue a forecast should make explicit.

---

## Limitations {#limitations}

1. **No external calibration.** Toronto 2026 has no published polling and we do not calibrate against historical election errors, so simulation win frequencies must not be quoted as real winning probabilities [@gelman2020information].
2. **Mayoral mode collapse** — 97.7% single-candidate concentration, invariant to ballot order — is a property of the models' world knowledge; the mayoral output is effectively single-candidate [@heath2026correcting].
3. **No turnout model.** Only 2 of 36,504 replies were "not voting"; turnout intent is not simulated, so results are decided-preference shares, not forecast valid-vote shares.
4. **Informative undecided responses.** GPT-4o-mini declines 19.4% of mayoral queries; exclusion without nonresponse adjustment conditions each provider on a different responder pool, and the exclusion mechanism itself may correlate with candidate preference [@bisbee2024synthetic].
5. **Census independence approximation.** Age × education cells within wards are built from marginal products, which can misallocate weight when the traits are correlated.
6. **Provider disagreement dominates method choices** in 8 of 25 wards — a single pooled forecast would hide genuine model uncertainty.
7. **Small effective samples** ($n_{\text{eff}}$ ≈ 79–165 in wards) give wide intervals; the Dirichlet +0.5 prior adds up to ≈ −4.7pp of leader shrinkage in the worst ward (draws only), and Method C is only approximately center-preserving (max realized bias 5.74pp) with an assumed, sensitivity-tested perturbation scale.
8. **Simulated voters are not voters.** The entire electorate is synthetic; the forecast measures what two LLMs say about a Census-shaped persona frame [@bisbee2024synthetic].

---

## Conclusion and Future Work {#conclusion}

Silicon sampling with census post-stratification can produce a complete, reproducible, openly documented forecast for all 26 Toronto municipal races from a $3.16 production run. What it produces is a measurement of two language models. Without news, the mayoral race is not a race in the models' world (Chow at 97.7% of valid responses, unchanged by ballot order); with a day's headlines, the entire synthetic electorate moves to whichever candidate the headlines favour. Ward races are more varied, and the two providers disagree about the leader in 8 of 25 wards, a model-uncertainty signal we report rather than average away. The uncertainty we report is explicitly layered and its assumptions (target SD) are sensitivity-tested, but it remains conditional on model outputs and uncalibrated to real election error.

Natural next steps, in order of value:

1. **Calibrate after 26 October.** Score every provider forecast against the official results with Brier and log scores, and measure the real coverage of the simulation intervals — turning the current honest disclaimer into an empirical error estimate.
2. **Model the undecided.** Treat "undecided" as an outcome to be modelled (e.g., a separate post-stratified rate with principled allocation) instead of dropping it.
3. **Correct mode collapse** following @heath2026correcting (semantic similarity rating) and re-test whether the mayoral race becomes informative.
4. **Strengthen the frame** by obtaining age × education joint counts (e.g., PUMF) to remove the independence approximation, and adding a turnout layer informed by @to2022turnout.
5. **Combine providers** with an explicit hierarchical model that treats provider as a random effect, instead of reporting arms separately.

---

## Reproducibility {#reproducibility}

**Repository:** <https://github.com/Sophiaaa12/toronto-election-forecast> — everything below runs from a fresh clone. The site is deployed with GitHub Pages from the `gh-pages` branch (built from `website/`); rendering makes no API calls and modifies no data.

### Complete workflow

``` bash
# 1. Data (official City of Toronto downloads, checksum-verified)
Rscript download_data.R && Rscript prepare_data.R

# 2. Population frame and synthetic personas (seeded)
Rscript R/run_pipeline.R

# 3. Silicon sampling (Python; requires OPENROUTER_API_KEY — NOT needed to
#    reproduce this site: all responses are committed and frozen)
python3 -m llm.runner run --selection head --repeats 3 --order random \
  --seed 20261026 --budget-usd 3.75

# 4. Post-stratification and Method C forecast draws (md5-guarded)
Rscript R/10_llm_poststratify.R processed/production/llm_responses.parquet centered

# 5. Tests (164 R expectations, 117 Python tests; no network)
Rscript tests/run_tests.R
python3 -m pytest tests/python -q

# 6. Website figures, tables, and site
Rscript website/make_figures.R
quarto render website
```

### Configuration actually used

| Setting | Value |
|---|---|
| Models | `google/gemini-2.5-flash-lite`, `openai/gpt-4o-mini` (via OpenRouter) |
| Prompt / temperature / max tokens | v1 / 0.7 / 256 |
| Repeats per persona-race-model | 3 |
| Ballot-order randomization seed | 20261026 |
| Forecast-draw seeds | base 245309; provider $m$ uses base $+ m$ |
| Draws per race × provider | 500 |
| Perturbation target SD | 0.04 (grid 0.02 / 0.04 / 0.06) |
| R packages | dplyr, tidyr, readr, readxl, jsonlite, nanoparquet, sf, ggplot2, scales, patchwork, ggrepel, ragg, systemfonts, testthat, styler (see [Software](#software)) |
| Python | 3.13 locally, 3.12 in GitHub Actions; requests, pyarrow, pytest |

### API costs

| Run | Requests | Cost (USD) |
|---|---|---|
| Production sampling (this forecast) | 36,504 | $3.1631 |
| All experiments (pilot + diagnostic + production) | 36,805 logged | $3.2004 |

Budget was capped at $3.75; spend is enforced per-request from `processed/llm/cost_log.jsonl` (git-ignored; committed summaries live in `processed/production/`). No credentials appear in the repository or on this site.

### Validation

The committed forecast passed **22/22 automated checks** (md5 preservation, 26 races / 243 candidates / 300 census cells, draw-simplex sums to 1 within $1.4\times10^{-15}$, win frequencies sum to 1 per race × provider, no NA/NaN, seed replay identity) — see `processed/forecast/validation_report.md`. Test suites: R 164/164 expectations across 7 files (testthat), Python 117/117 (pytest).

### AI-use declaration

We used three AI tools. All code they produced was read, run, and tested by us before it was committed, and we can explain each script.

- **OpenCode with MiMo-V2.6-Flash (Xiaomi, free tier; model identifier `mimo-v2.6-flash`), 17–19 October 2026.** Jingwen Zhong used it as a coding agent to write and test the OpenRouter query pipeline (`llm/`), the simulated-data pipeline and its tests (`R/07`–`R/10`, `R/simulation_helpers.R`, `tests/testthat/test-07` to `test-11`, `tests/python/`), the ballot-order diagnostic (`scripts/analyze_llm_diagnostic.py`, `docs/`), the uncertainty comparison (`experiments/`), and the first version of the website and `website/make_figures.R`.
- **Claude Code with Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic; model identifier `claude-opus-5-5`), 19 and 22 October 2026.** Jingwen Zhong used it as a coding agent to fix and redesign the website figures and tables (`website/make_figures.R`, `website/make_daily.R`), build the shared design system (`website/theme_site.R`, `website/custom.scss`), add the software citations, remove `setwd()` from scripts and tests, run styler, add the submission-deadline guard to the GitHub Action, and review the project against the rubric. It also drafted website prose: the Discussion section, figure and table captions, the "What the model sees" and Software subsections, and edits to the Overview and Daily Tracker text. We checked every number in that prose against our data and edited it.
- **ChatGPT with GPT-5.6 (OpenAI; model identifier `gpt-5.6`).** Siyi Zhu used it for TODO (Siyi: list the scripts or tasks, e.g. `download_data.R`, `R/01`–`R/06`, `R/11`–`R/12`, the daily tracker, the GitHub Action, and the dates).

The two language models that generate the synthetic responses, `openai/gpt-4o-mini` and `google/gemini-2.5-flash-lite` via OpenRouter, are the object of study rather than writing aids; every response they returned is kept in the repository.
